nameStory: The "modest" sphinx gets its name from its understated, muted coloration compared to many of its flashier sphinx moth relatives. While some sphinx moths sport bold patterns and bright colors, this species keeps a low profile with subtle browns and grays that help it blend seamlessly into tree bark. It's also called the poplar sphinx because its caterpillars feed primarily on poplar and aspen trees.
description: The Modest Sphinx is a medium to large moth with a wingspan of about 3-4 inches, making it smaller than some of its sphinx moth cousins but still substantial enough to be mistaken for a small bird in flight. Its wings are painted in soft browns, grays, and tans with intricate wavy lines and subtle patterns that look like wood grain. Like all sphinx moths, it has a thick, fuzzy body and triangular wings that it holds horizontally when at rest. The adults are most active at dusk and nighttime, when they hover at flowers to feed on nectar with their long tongues.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for wavy, irregular lines across brownish-gray wings that create a wood-grain or tree bark pattern - run your eyes along these zigzag markings that seem to ripple across the wing surface

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Notice the thick, torpedo-shaped body covered in dense, soft fur-like scales that feel velvety to the touch if you can examine a specimen closely

idTips.label: Flight Style
idTips.description: Watch for the characteristic hovering flight at flowers, wings beating so rapidly they become a blur while the moth hangs motionless in the air like a hummingbird

idTips.label: Wing Position at Rest
idTips.description: When landed, the wings are held horizontally outward from the body rather than folded back like a butterfly, creating a triangular silhouette

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-large moth with wings spanning about the width of your palm when fully extended, noticeably smaller than the massive Cecropia or Luna moths

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Thick, slightly feathered antennae that taper to pointed tips, quite different from the thread-like antennae of smaller moths

habitat: Look for Modest Sphinx moths in areas with poplar, aspen, and willow trees, as these are the host plants for their caterpillars. They're found in mixed woodlands, forest edges, parks, and suburban areas throughout New England, especially where these trees grow near gardens or wildflower patches. Adults are drawn to night-blooming flowers and will visit suburban gardens with petunias, honeysuckle, or other fragrant evening flowers.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, usually May, when you might spot them at dusk visiting early flowering trees and shrubs. This is when mated females are laying eggs on young poplar and aspen leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time is early to mid-summer (June-July) when adults are most active and easiest to spot hovering at flowers during twilight hours. Look for the large green caterpillars with diagonal white stripes on poplar trees during this time.
seasonality.fall: A second generation of adults may appear in late summer to early fall in warmer years. Caterpillars are preparing to pupate in the soil, so you won't see the adults flying around much by September.
seasonality.winter: Pupae overwinter buried in the soil beneath host trees, completely hidden from view until the following spring's emergence.

funFact: Modest Sphinx caterpillars can make a loud clicking sound when threatened by grinding their mandibles together - a sound so distinct that experienced naturalists can identify the species just by listening to this defensive "chatter" without even seeing the caterpillar!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other brown sphinx moths, especially the One-eyed Sphinx, but the Modest Sphinx lacks the distinctive blue "eye spot" on the hindwing. Memory trick: "Modest" moths don't show off with flashy eye spots - they keep their wings plain and understated.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "modest," these moths are actually quite bold in their feeding behavior, fearlessly hovering at flowers even when humans are nearby. The scientific name Pachysphinx means "thick sphinx," referring to their robust, chunky build compared to other sphinx moths.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus Pachysphinx in New England, the Modest Sphinx is most similar to other brown sphinx moths in the family. However, it's distinguished by its particularly thick, robust body and the specific wavy, wood-grain pattern on its wings. Unlike the Wild Cherry Sphinx or One-eyed Sphinx, it lacks prominent eye spots or bold contrasting colors, staying true to its "modest" name with consistently muted, bark-like tones.
